lesson.body:
It all starts in the vineyard. When the grapes are ripe and sweet, they're picked, then crushed and pressed to squeeze out the juice. For white wine, the juice is separated from the skins right away; for red wine, the juice stays in contact with the dark skins, which is where the color comes from.

Next comes fermentation, the heart of winemaking. Tiny living organisms called yeast eat the natural sugar in the juice and convert it into alcohol, a bit like how bread dough rises. When the yeast finishes its work, the sweet juice has become wine. The wine then rests, or "ages," to develop flavor. This can happen in steel tanks, which keep it fresh and fruity, or in wooden barrels, which add gentle notes like vanilla or spice.

Before bottling, the wine is clarified, meaning the leftover bits and cloudiness are removed so it pours clear and bright. Finally it's sealed in bottles, ready to travel from the winery to your glass.
outcomes: Describe how grapes become juice, and where colour comes from
Explain how yeast turns grape juice into wine
Compare ageing in steel tanks and wooden barrels

steps.body: Ripe, sweet grapes are picked, then crushed and pressed for their juice. For white wine, the juice is separated from the skins right away. For red, it stays with the dark skins, which give the colour.
steps.title: Juice comes from pressing, colour from skins

steps.q: Which steps squeeze the juice out of ripe grapes?
steps.why: Ripe grapes are crushed and pressed to squeeze out the juice. Fermenting and clarifying come later.

steps.q: Red wine gets its colour from the dark grape skins.
steps.why: For red wine, the juice stays in contact with the dark skins. For white, it's separated from them right away.

steps.body: Fermentation, the heart of winemaking, is when yeast (tiny living organisms) eat the natural sugar in the juice and turn it into alcohol. When the yeast finishes, the sweet juice has become wine.
steps.tip: Think of bread dough rising. Yeast is busy there too, a bit like it is in wine.
steps.title: Yeast turns sugar into alcohol

steps.q: Yeast eats the natural sugar in grape juice. What does it turn that sugar into?
steps.why: Yeast converts the natural sugar into alcohol. When it finishes, the sweet juice has become wine.

steps.body: After fermentation, wine rests, or ages, to develop flavour. Steel tanks keep it fresh and fruity. Wooden barrels add gentle notes like vanilla or spice.
steps.tip: Notice a gentle hint of vanilla or spice in a wine? Wooden barrels can add that.
steps.title: Steel keeps it fruity, wood adds vanilla

steps.q: Wooden barrels keep a wine fresh and fruity.
steps.why: That's what steel tanks do. Wooden barrels add gentle notes like vanilla or spice.

steps.body: Before bottling, the wine is clarified. That means the leftover bits and cloudiness are removed, so it pours clear and bright. Then it's sealed in bottles, ready to travel to your glass.
steps.title: Wine is made clear before bottling

steps.q: What does clarifying do to a wine?
steps.why: Clarifying removes the leftover bits and cloudiness, so the wine pours clear and bright before it's bottled.

bank.q: You are making a white wine. What happens to the juice and the skins?
bank.why: For white wine, the juice leaves the skins straight away, so it takes no colour from them.

bank.q: For red wine, the juice is separated from the skins straight away.
bank.why: That is how white wine is made. For red, the juice stays with the dark skins, and they give it colour.

bank.q: Which of these are the first steps in making wine?
bank.why: It all starts with picking ripe, sweet grapes, then crushing and pressing them for juice. Clarifying and bottling come at the very end.

bank.q: Which everyday food also relies on busy yeast?
bank.why: Yeast makes bread dough rise. In wine, yeast is busy too, turning sugar into alcohol.

bank.q: The sugar that yeast turns into alcohol is already in the grape juice.
bank.why: Ripe grapes are naturally sweet. Yeast eats that natural sugar and turns it into alcohol.

bank.q: Which of these are true about fermentation?
bank.why: Yeast eats the sugar and turns it into alcohol, and that is how juice becomes wine. The juice gets less sweet, not more.

opts: Only once the bottle is opened
bank.q: When does a wine rest, or age, to develop its flavour?
bank.why: Ageing comes after fermentation. The new wine rests so its flavour can develop.

bank.q: A wine that rested in a steel tank is likely to taste fresh and fruity.
bank.why: Steel tanks keep a wine fresh and fruity. Notes like vanilla or spice come from wooden barrels instead.

opts: It rested in a steel tank
The juice stayed with the skins
It rested in a wooden barrel
bank.q: You notice a gentle hint of vanilla in a wine. What is the likely reason?
bank.why: Wooden barrels add gentle notes like vanilla or spice. Steel tanks keep the fruit to the fore instead.

bank.q: Clarifying happens after the wine is sealed in bottles.
bank.why: It is the other way round. The wine is clarified first, so it pours clear and bright, and then it is bottled.

bank.q: A wine pours clear and bright. Which step made it that way?
bank.why: Clarifying removes the leftover bits and cloudiness, which is why the wine looks clear and bright.

bank.q: Which of these come after fermentation?
bank.why: Picking and crushing happen before the yeast gets to work. Clarifying and bottling are the last steps before the wine leaves the winery.

deep_notes: Many wineries first destem the bunches, because the stalks can taste green and bitter. Crushing then gently splits the skins, and some juice runs out under the grapes' own weight. This free-run juice is usually the most delicate. Pressing squeezes out the rest, which carries more tannin, the drying grip that comes from skins and pips. One twist: for red wine, the pressing usually comes after fermentation.

Yeast splits sugar into two main products: alcohol and carbon dioxide, a gas that usually just bubbles away. The process also gives off heat, so winemakers often cool their tanks to keep it steady. Some rely on wild yeasts, the ones that live naturally on grape skins and in the cellar. Others add cultured yeasts, strains chosen because they work reliably. Most fermentations last from about a week to a few weeks.

Stainless steel is inert, meaning it adds no flavour of its own, and a sealed tank keeps air out, which protects the fresh fruit aromas. Wood works differently. The vanilla note comes from a natural compound in oak called vanillin, and coopers, the craftspeople who make barrels, toast the inside over a fire, which brings the spicy, toasty notes. A classic Bordeaux barrel, the barrique, holds 225 litres.

Winemakers clarify in a few ways. Racking means moving the wine off the sediment that has sunk to the bottom of the tank or barrel. Fining adds an agent such as egg white or bentonite, a kind of clay, which grabs tiny particles so they drop out. Filtering strains the wine through a fine filter. Some producers skip fining and filtering, so their wines can look slightly hazy or leave a little sediment in the bottle.

deeper.body: As grapes ripen, their sugar rises and their acidity falls. Pick too early and the wine tastes thin and sour. Pick too late and it can taste jammy, with high alcohol and little freshness. Growers taste the grapes and measure their sugar, often with a refractometer, a small tool that reads the sugar level from a single drop of juice.
deeper.title: Picking day is a balancing act

opts: Both stay the same until picking
deeper.q: What happens to grapes as they ripen on the vine?
deeper.why: Ripening grapes gain sugar and lose acidity. Picking day is about catching the right balance between the two.

deeper.body: Sometimes yeast stops before the sugar is gone. Winemakers call this a stuck fermentation. Common causes are a tank that gets too hot, too few nutrients for the yeast, or very ripe juice that makes so much alcohol the yeast cannot carry on. An unfinished wine with leftover sugar is food for spoilage bacteria, so it needs fixing fast.
deeper.title: When the yeast gives up early

opts: A tank that gets too hot
Too few nutrients for the yeast
Resting the wine in steel afterwards
deeper.q: Which of these can cause a stuck fermentation?
deeper.why: Heat, hungry yeast and very sugary juice can all stall a fermentation. Where the wine rests afterwards has nothing to do with it.

deeper.body: Even a clear wine can later show tiny glassy crystals on the cork or at the bottom of the bottle. These are tartrates, often called wine diamonds. They form from tartaric acid, the main acid in grapes, when the wine gets cold. Many wineries chill their wine close to freezing before bottling, so the crystals form in the tank instead. This is called cold stabilisation.
deeper.title: Wine diamonds are harmless

deeper.q: Tartrate crystals in a bottle are a sign that the wine has gone bad.
deeper.why: Tartrates are harmless crystals from the grape's own tartaric acid. They simply show the wine got cold at some point.

bank.key: Sealed steel tanks keep a wine fresh and fruity; oak barrels add notes like vanilla or spice.
bank.q: Oak barrels keep a wine fresher and fruitier than sealed steel tanks.
bank.remember: Steel keeps it fresh; oak adds spice.
bank.why: Where the wine rests shapes its taste: steel protects the fruit, oak adds its own flavours.

bank.key: Filtering removes yeast and bacteria before bottling, so they cannot spoil the wine in the bottle.
bank.q: Filtering strains out yeast and bacteria that could spoil a wine later.
bank.remember: Filter out the troublemakers before the cork goes in.
bank.why: Yeast or bacteria left in a bottled wine could start working again and spoil it.

bank.key: After fermentation the new wine settles, and the clear wine is moved off its sediment.
bank.q: Of these steps, which comes next after fermentation?
bank.remember: Ferment, then settle: the sludge comes off first.
bank.why: Every wine follows the same order: crush, ferment, settle and rest, finish, bottle.

bank.key: White grapes are pressed at once; red wine ferments with its skins and is pressed afterwards.
bank.q: Red wine is pressed after fermentation, white wine before it.
bank.remember: White presses first, red presses last.
bank.why: Colour and tannin, the drying feel of strong tea, sit in the skins, so only a red needs that long contact.

bank.key: For white wine the grapes are pressed straight away and only the juice ferments.
bank.q: Which of these are true of making white wine?
bank.remember: White wine leaves its skins at the press.
bank.why: Without time on the skins, a white stays pale and takes little tannin, the drying feel in your mouth.

bank.key: Sugar becomes roughly half alcohol and half carbon dioxide by weight.
bank.q: By weight, roughly how much of the fermented sugar becomes carbon dioxide?
bank.why: That is a lot of gas: in a closed bottle it is what makes sparkling wine fizz.

bank.key: In both, yeast feeds on sugar and gives off carbon dioxide; in wine the alcohol stays.
bank.q: The yeast in wine works a bit like the yeast that makes bread rise.
bank.remember: Bread rises, wine ferments: same yeast family.
bank.why: The same busy organism raises dough and turns grape juice into wine.

bank.key: Wild yeasts live on the grape skins and in the cellar.
bank.q: Where do wild yeasts come from?
bank.remember: Wild yeast rides in on the grapes.
bank.why: Cultured yeast is one chosen type, added dried; wild yeast arrives on its own, trading control for character.

bank.key: Cultured yeast is a chosen strain that starts fast and finishes reliably.
opts: It gives the wine its red colour
It starts fast and finishes reliably
It adds vanilla and spice notes
bank.q: Why might a winemaker choose cultured yeast?
bank.remember: Cultured yeast: the safe pair of hands.
bank.why: A predictable fermentation lowers the risk of yeast stopping early or of off flavours.

bank.key: The lees are the dead yeast and grape bits that sink; racking moves the clear wine off them.
bank.q: The lees are the clear wine left after racking.
bank.remember: Lees sink; the wine moves on.
bank.why: Knowing the word helps with labels that say sur lie (French for 'on the lees'): wines rested on them on purpose.

bank.key: Beaujolais Nouveau is sold just weeks after the harvest, made to drink young.
bank.q: Which wine is usually sold just weeks after the harvest?
bank.remember: Nouveau: the fastest trip from vine to glass.
bank.why: Resting time depends on the style: light, fruity wines need little, fine reds a year or more.

bank.key: Bentonite, a clay, removes proteins that can make a white wine cloudy.
bank.q: What does bentonite remove from a white wine?
bank.why: Without it, some whites turn hazy later, for example after a warm spell.

bank.key: Some fining agents, such as egg white, come from animals, so not every wine is vegan.
bank.q: Every wine is vegan, because wine is made only from grapes.
bank.remember: Made from grapes, sometimes cleared with egg.
bank.why: The egg white sinks and is removed, but vegans may still want a wine labelled vegan.

bank.key: Sulphur dioxide, often added at the crush and before bottling, guards wine against air and bacteria.
opts: To give the wine gentle bubbles
To guard against air and bacteria
To deepen the wine's red colour
To add a little extra sweetness
bank.q: Why is sulphur dioxide added to wine?
bank.why: It keeps the wine sound on its long trip from the winery to your glass.

v2.body:
In 1897 a German scientist, **Eduard Buchner**, ground yeast, the tiny living things that turn sugar into alcohol, with sand. He squeezed out a juice with no living yeast in it, yet sugar stirred into it still fermented. The work was done by **enzymes**, chemicals inside the yeast that act like tiny tools; he called them zymase. Pasteur had shown that living yeast makes wine. Buchner showed that chemicals inside it do the work, and won the 1907 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

On harvest day the grapes are sorted, usually destemmed and crushed to split the skins. For white wine the grapes are pressed at once and only the juice ferments. For red wine the juice ferments with its skins, which give colour and tannin, the drying feel of strong tea, and the pressing comes after.

**Fermentation** is the heart of it: yeast eats the grapes' natural sugar and turns it into alcohol, a bit like the yeast that makes bread rise. By weight, the sugar becomes roughly half alcohol and half carbon dioxide, a gas that bubbles away. Fermenting gives off heat, so winemakers cool their tanks: too hot, and the yeast can stall with sugar left unfermented, a stuck fermentation. It usually lasts from about a week to a few weeks. The winemaker also chooses the yeast. **Wild yeast** lives on grape skins and in the cellar: several kinds start, and the hardiest finishes. Cultured yeast is one chosen strain, added as dried yeast, for a fast, reliable start.

Next the new wine settles. Dead yeast and grape bits sink to the bottom as the **lees**, and the clear wine is moved off them into a clean vessel, often more than once. This is **racking**. Then the wine rests, or ages, to develop flavour: sealed steel tanks keep it fresh and fruity, while oak barrels add notes like vanilla or spice. Beaujolais Nouveau, a light French red, is sold just weeks after the harvest, many fresh whites within months, and many fine reds a year or more.

Before bottling, the wine is made clear and stable. **Fining** adds something that grabs tiny particles so they sink: egg white softens a red's tannin, and bentonite, a clay, removes proteins that can cloud a white. Some of these come from animals, so not every wine is vegan; in the EU, egg or milk used must be declared if detectable. Filtering strains out yeast and bacteria. **Cold stabilisation** chills the wine near freezing, so harmless tartrate crystals form in the tank, not on your cork. Sulphur dioxide, a preservative often added at the crush and before bottling, guards against air and bacteria. Some producers skip fining and filtering, so their wines can look slightly hazy. Finally it is bottled, ready to travel to your glass.
deep_notes: The scientist was Eduard Buchner, and the discovery began almost by accident. The juice was meant for medical research, and, as the story is usually told, the team stirred in sugar to help keep it, as you would to make jam. It began to bubble. It still fermented after every cell was filtered out. Buchner called the active stuff zymase and won the 1907 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. Today we know zymase is a whole team of enzymes.

Many wineries first destem the bunches, because stalks can taste green and bitter, though some keep whole bunches on purpose. Crushing then gently splits the skins so the juice can run. Juice that runs out under the grapes' own weight, before any pressing, is called free-run juice and is usually the most delicate. Pressing squeezes out the rest, which carries more tannin from the skins and pips.

Pressing is the moment the two roads part for good. For a white, the press comes first, and the skins, seeds and stems go no further. For a red, the skins, seeds and new wine sit together in the tank through fermentation; only then does the press squeeze out the wine soaked into the skins. That is why a red press handles a mass of soft, wine-soaked skins rather than whole grapes.

Chemists write fermentation as one molecule of glucose becoming two of alcohol and two of carbon dioxide. A real tank is a little less tidy. Yeast also makes glycerol, which adds a touch of smoothness, plus small amounts of acids and aroma compounds, and some sugar feeds the yeast's own growth. That is why wine scientists reckon on about 17 grams of sugar per litre for each 1% of alcohol.

In a wild ferment, several kinds of yeast from the vineyard begin, among them Hanseniaspora (once called Kloeckera), Candida and Pichia. As alcohol builds, Saccharomyces cerevisiae, the hardiest, takes over and finishes. Wild yeasts reach a tank on grape skins, on harvest bins, in the air and even on fruit flies. Cultured strains are tested in laboratories for traits such as a steady start and tolerance of alcohol, and are sold dried, to be woken in warm water.

The first racking usually comes soon after fermentation, to take the wine off the heavy, or gross, lees. Left too long on a thick, undisturbed layer, wine can pick up stale, eggy sulphur smells. The fine lees that settle later are gentler, and some winemakers keep a wine on them on purpose for a creamy texture: known as sur lie ageing, sometimes with stirring, or bâtonnage. Racking also gives the wine a small breath of air.

Resting is not idle time. The young wine's harsh edges soften and its flavours knit together, while fine particles keep settling, so it may be racked again. Stainless steel is inert, adding no flavour of its own, and a sealed tank keeps air out, protecting fresh fruit; concrete tanks and clay jars are other choices. Wood both flavours a wine and lets it breathe. Beaujolais Nouveau, sold within weeks, has one of the shortest rests of all.

Fining works by attraction. Egg white proteins bind to the harshest tannins in a red, while bentonite's clay particles, which carry a negative electric charge, swell in the wine and grab the positively charged proteins, so the clumps grow heavy and sink. Other agents include casein from milk, isinglass from fish bladders, gelatin and activated charcoal. The agent settles out and is racked or filtered away; studies usually find only traces, if any, in the finished wine. Too much fining can also strip aroma.

Filters come in two broad kinds. Thick pads of cellulose or diatomaceous earth trap particles in their depth, while thin membranes act like a very fine sieve; the finest hold back yeast and bacteria, which matters most for wines with sugar left in them. Cold stabilisation often keeps the wine near freezing for a week or more. A little sulphur dioxide forms during fermentation anyway, so almost no wine is entirely free of it.

deeper.body: Grapes carry natural proteins that stay dissolved in a young white wine. Warm the bottle, in a hot car or a sunny shop window, and they can clump into a cloudy haze. It is harmless and barely changes the taste, but it looks faulty. So winemakers test: they heat samples with rising doses of bentonite and choose the smallest dose that stays clear, because too much clay also strips aroma. Reds rarely need this, as their tannins already pull the proteins out.
deeper.title: Protein haze waits for a warm day

deeper.key: Samples are heated with rising doses of bentonite, and the smallest dose that stays clear is chosen.
opts: They taste the grapes at harvest
They heat samples with rising doses
They always use the largest dose
They wait for haze in the bottle
deeper.q: How do winemakers pick the dose of bentonite for a white wine?
deeper.remember: Heat-test first, then add just enough clay.
deeper.why: Too little leaves the wine at risk of haze; too much strips aroma along with the proteins.

deeper.body: Sulphur dioxide does not all stay on duty. Part of it binds to other compounds in the wine, and only the free part protects against air and microbes. So winemakers measure the free part and top it up when needed. Reds usually need less than whites, because their skin compounds are natural antioxidants. In the EU and the USA, a label must mention sulphites once a wine holds more than about 10 milligrams per litre, which covers almost every wine.
deeper.title: Only the free sulphur dioxide stands guard

deeper.key: Part of the sulphur dioxide binds to other compounds; only the free part guards against air and microbes.
deeper.q: Only the free part of a wine's sulphur dioxide protects it.
deeper.remember: Bound is off duty; free stands guard.
deeper.why: That is why winemakers measure the free part, not just the total, before bottling.

deeper.body: Some producers print unfined or unfiltered on the label. They argue that every treatment strips a little aroma or texture, and that a wine left alone tastes fuller. The trade-off is risk: without filtering, yeast or bacteria left in a wine with any sugar could start working again in the bottle. Such wines may look slightly hazy or throw a sediment over the years, so pour them gently or decant them.
deeper.title: Unfined and unfiltered: a label promise

deeper.key: Unfiltered wines can look slightly hazy and may throw a sediment as they age.
deeper.q: What can you expect from a wine labelled unfiltered?
deeper.remember: Unfiltered: pour slowly, leave the last drop.
deeper.why: Pour gently or decant, so the sediment stays in the bottle rather than your glass.
